p: The Greek translates the name as "Baal Fly," and Josephus calls him the "god of flies."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); KJV and modern versions
Septuagint (Greek); compare Josephus, Antiquities 9.2.1
readings.plain: Baal the Fly, the god of Ekron

why: This is not a different Hebrew text but a translation of the name. The Plain English keeps the name as a name and explains it in a note. The Greek shows that ancient readers already understood zevuv as "fly."

p: The Hebrew says the second captain "answered"; the Greek says he "went up," as the other two captains do.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
Septuagint (Greek, ἀνέβη); many commentators, who restore Hebrew וַיַּעַל

why: The two Hebrew words differ by one letter (vayya'an, "he answered," and vayya'al, "he went up"). "Answered" is odd, since no one has spoken to him, but Hebrew often uses "answer" for beginning to speak. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew; the Greek reading fits the pattern of 1:9 and 1:13 and may be original.

a: Jehoram became king in his place, in the second year of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, because Ahaziah had no son.
p: The Greek ends 1:17 with Elijah's word. It has no date for Jehoram's reign here and gives one after 1:18 instead.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Targum; Vulgate
readings.orig: וַיִּמְלֹךְ יְהוֹרָם תַּחְתָּיו בִּשְׁנַת שְׁתַּיִם לִיהוֹרָם
readings.en: and Jehoram became king in his place in the second year of Jehoram ...
readings.plain: Jehoram became king in his place, in the second year of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, because Ahaziah had no son.

readings.w: Septuagint, Codex Vaticanus (Rahlfs); the Lucianic text was not checked directly
readings.orig: καὶ ἀπέθανεν κατὰ τὸ ῥῆμα κυρίου ὃ ἐλάλησεν Ηλιου
readings.en: and he died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah spoke (the verse ends here)

why: The Hebrew dates the accession of Jehoram of Israel to the second year of Jehoram of Judah, which conflicts with 3:1 (the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat). The Greek lacks the date and the succession clause and gives instead, after 1:18, a notice that agrees with 3:1. The two Greek differences belong together. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew, the harder reading, which most scholars explain by a co-regency of Jehoram of Judah with his father. The Greek looks like a smoothing of the chronology, though Shenkel argued that the Old Greek kept an older system of dates.

a: The rest of Ahaziah's story, what he did, is written down, isn't it, in the scroll of the day-by-day records of the kings of Israel?
p: The Greek adds after 1:18 a summary of Jehoram's reign, dated as in 3:1. It goes with the shorter Greek 1:17.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum; Vulgate; KJV and modern versions
readings.en: The rest of the matters of Ahaziah ... the kings of Israel
readings.plain: The rest of Ahaziah's story, what he did, is written down, isn't it, in the scroll of the day-by-day records of the kings of Israel?

readings.w: Septuagint (4 Kingdoms 1:18a–d in Rahlfs), in the main Greek manuscripts
readings.orig: καὶ Ιωραμ υἱὸς Αχααβ βασιλεύει ἐπὶ Ισραηλ ...
readings.en: And Joram son of Ahab reigned over Israel in Samaria twelve years, in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah ...
readings.plain: The rest of Ahaziah's story, what he did, is written down, isn't it, in the scroll of the day-by-day records of the kings of Israel? Joram son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he ruled for twelve years. He did what the LORD sees as evil, but not like his brothers or like his mother. He took away the standing stones of Baal that his father had made and broke them. But he held to the sins of the house of Jeroboam, who led Israel into sin; he did not turn from them. And the LORD was furious with the house of Ahab.

why: The Plain English follows the Hebrew. The Greek plus repeats 3:1–3 with small differences ("his brothers" for "his father," "pillars" in the plural, and a closing line about the LORD's anger), and it looks like a regnal summary placed where the Greek editors expected it, right after Ahaziah's death. It works together with the Greek of 1:17, which lacks the Hebrew's date for Jehoram's accession (see the variant there): the Greek replaces a date that conflicts with 3:1 with one that agrees with it. The Greek wording shown is a summary of Rahlfs' text, not a full quotation.
b: All of 2 Kings belongs to the "kaige" section of the Greek, where the main manuscript, Codex Vaticanus (and so Rahlfs), has a text revised toward the Hebrew. The Lucianic (Antiochene) manuscripts are the better witness to the Old Greek here. That even the revised Greek keeps this plus suggests it is old. Some scholars (Shenkel) think the Old Greek had its own chronology for the Omride kings and that pluses like this one and 1 Kings 16:28a–h come from it; others think they are later harmonizing additions. The Lucianic readings were not checked line by line for this note.

a: he said. "Yes, where is he?" He struck
p: Two small Hebrew words can end the question or begin the next clause. The Greek also has a first strike that fails.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, as its accents divide the verse
readings.plain: he said. "Yes, where is he?" He struck

readings.w: KJV and some interpreters, joining the words to what follows
readings.plain: he said. When he too struck

readings.w: Septuagint, Codex Vaticanus (Rahlfs), which also has a failed first strike and "the God of Elijah" without "the LORD"; the Lucianic text was not checked directly
readings.orig: καὶ ἐπάταξεν τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ οὐ διέστη καὶ εἶπεν ποῦ ὁ θεὸς Ηλιου αφφω καὶ ἐπάταξεν τὰ ὕδατα
readings.en: and he struck the water, and it did not part; and he said, "Where is the God of Elijah, aphphō?" and he struck the waters

why: The Masoretic accents put 'af hu', "even he," with the question, as an emphatic "yes, he," and the Plain English follows them. The KJV reads "when he also had smitten the waters," taking the words as "he too" with the next verb. The Greek translator did not understand them and copied the sounds into Greek letters. The Greek also tells the scene differently: Elisha strikes the water once and it does not part; then he asks, "Where is the God of Elijah?" and strikes again, and the water splits. The Plain English keeps the shorter Hebrew. The Greek plus may be an attempt to explain why the Hebrew says "he struck the water" twice, and it makes Elisha's question follow a failure. Some scholars restore a different small word for 'af hu', such as "now" or "then."

a: Israel pushed on into the land
p: The written Hebrew (Ketiv) says Israel "went into" Moab; the Masoretes' reading (Qere) says they "struck" it.

readings.w: Ketiv (the consonants written in the Leningrad Codex), read וַיָּבוֹאוּ בָהּ; supported by the Greek, which has Israel "going in"
readings.plain: Israel pushed on into the land

readings.w: Qere (the reading the Masoretes marked to be spoken); KJV "went forward smiting"

why: The two readings differ by one letter. The Ketiv fits the story, which goes on to describe the army destroying towns, fields, springs and trees inside Moab (3:25). The Qere is an attempt to smooth an unclear form. Both end the same way: "striking Moab." The Plain English follows the Ketiv, with most modern versions.

p: The Greek renders qetsef as "great regret" (metamelos), as if Israel was sorry for what it had caused.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Targum; Vulgate (indignatio magna); KJV "great indignation"
Septuagint (Greek; the kaige text of Codex Vaticanus as printed in Rahlfs)

why: This is a difference of translation, not of the Hebrew letters. The Greek translator seems to have taken the wrath as a human reaction, perhaps to avoid saying that Moab's god, or the LORD, struck Israel. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew word, which elsewhere almost always means God's wrath, and leaves its source open as the Hebrew does.

p: In the Greek Elisha crouches over the boy seven times, and there is no sneeze.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Targum; Vulgate
readings.en: and the boy sneezed up to seven times

readings.w: Septuagint, Codex Vaticanus (Rahlfs); the Lucianic text was not checked directly
readings.orig: καὶ συνέκαμψεν ἐπὶ τὸ παιδάριον ἕως ἑπτάκις
readings.en: and he bowed over the child up to seven times
readings.plain: He crouched over the boy seven times

why: The Hebrew verb zarar, "sneeze," appears only here. The Greek translator may not have known it, and so joined "seven times" to the crouching before it. The rare word is the harder reading, and it is hard to see why a scribe would invent it. The Plain English follows the Hebrew.

p: The written Hebrew has Abana; the Masoretes' reading has Amana, a name of a mountain in Song of Songs 4:8.

readings.w: Ketiv (the written consonants); Septuagint (Greek Abana); KJV and most versions
Qere (the reading the Masoretes marked to be spoken); Targum

why: The letters b and m sound alike and were often exchanged. "Amana" is the name of a peak in the Anti-Lebanon (Song of Songs 4:8), where the river rises, so either name fits. The Plain English follows the written text and most translations.

p: The written text says "dove's dung." The Masoretes told readers to say a politer word, and some think it is a plant name.

readings.w: Ketiv (the written consonants); Septuagint (Greek, "dung of doves"); KJV
Qere (the reading the Masoretes marked to be spoken), a polite substitute
Some interpreters and versions (NIV "seed pods"), taking it as a plant name

why: The Masoretes often marked a more modest word to be read aloud in place of a crude one (compare 18:27). That does not change the meaning. Some scholars think "dove's dung" was a popular name for a plant, such as carob pods or the bulb called star-of-Bethlehem, which the poor ate in famine. Others take it literally, as food or fuel in desperation. The Plain English follows the written text.

p: The Greek prices the donkey's head at fifty shekels of silver, not eighty.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Targum; Vulgate
Septuagint, Codex Vaticanus (Rahlfs); the Lucianic text was not checked directly

why: Numbers were easily confused in copying. Neither figure can be shown to be original, and either one is a famine price. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew.

a: the messenger came down to him
p: The Hebrew says "the messenger" came down. Many scholars think it originally said "the king," who speaks next and is with Elisha in 7:2.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Septuagint; KJV
readings.plain: the messenger came down to him

readings.w: Conjectural emendation adopted by many commentators (a small change of letters)
readings.plain: the king came down to him

why: "Messenger" (mal'akh) and "king" (melekh) have the same consonants except one letter. The words that follow, "this disaster is the LORD's doing," fit the king better than a servant, and in 7:2 the king's officer is present and in 7:17 the text says "the king went down" to Elisha. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew, since no manuscript has "king," and leaves the speaker unnamed, as the Hebrew does.

a: Look, they are like the whole crowd of Israel still left in the town. Look, they are like the whole crowd of Israel already gone.
p: The Hebrew has two almost identical clauses. Some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions have only one.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); KJV
readings.orig: הִנָּם כְּכָל־הֲמוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר נִשְׁאֲרוּ־בָהּ הִנָּם כְּכָל־הֲמוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר־תָּמּוּ
readings.en: they are like all the multitude of Israel that are left in it ... they are like all the multitude of Israel that are consumed
readings.plain: Look, they are like the whole crowd of Israel still left in the town. Look, they are like the whole crowd of Israel already gone.

readings.w: Some Hebrew manuscripts, Septuagint, Syriac and Vulgate, as reported in BHS
readings.en: (the clause about those left in the town is lacking)
readings.plain: Look, they are like the whole crowd of Israel already gone.

why: The two clauses differ only in their last word, "left" and "gone." The first may have come in by a copyist's eye slipping between similar lines, and the shorter text reads more smoothly: the horses "will only perish like the rest." But the longer text makes good sense too: whether the horses stay in the starving city or go out, they face death, so nothing is lost by sending them. The Plain English follows the Hebrew. The witnesses for the shorter text are given here as the standard apparatus reports them; they were not checked one by one.

a: Go and tell him, 'You are sure to live.'
p: The Hebrew word lo can mean "not" or "to him." The written text has "not"; the Masoretes read "to him."

readings.w: Qere (the reading the Masoretes marked to be spoken); KJV and most versions
readings.en: say to him, You will surely live
readings.plain: Go and tell him, 'You are sure to live.'

readings.w: Ketiv (the written consonants of the Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: say: You will surely not live
readings.plain: Go and say, 'You will certainly not live.'

why: The two words sound the same (lo) and were often confused. The Ketiv removes any hint of deception, which may be why some scholars think it was a scribal correction. The Qere fits 8:14, where Hazael reports "You are sure to live," and the contrast with the next clause, "but the LORD has shown me he is sure to die." The Plain English follows the Qere with most versions.

p: These words, which suggest that father and son ruled together, are missing from the Greek and some other witnesses.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); KJV
Septuagint, Codex Vaticanus (Rahlfs); also reported for the Lucianic Greek, the Syriac Peshitta and some Hebrew manuscripts (as BHS gives them, not checked directly); many modern scholars

why: Many scholars think the phrase is a copyist's repetition of "king of Judah" from the end of the verse. Others, especially those who build the chronology on co-regencies (Thiele), see it as a sign that Jehoram began to rule while his father was still alive. The Plain English keeps the Hebrew. Both Greek traditions lack the phrase: even the kaige text of Vaticanus, which was revised toward the Hebrew, does not have it, and the Lucianic text, the better witness to the Old Greek here, is reported to lack it too. That gives the shorter text real weight.

p: Kings says the lamp is "for his sons"; Chronicles and some manuscripts say "to him and to his sons."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
2 Chronicles 21:7; some Hebrew manuscripts and versions

why: The difference is one letter, a "and." With it, the lamp is given to David and to his sons; without it, the lamp is given to David, through his sons. The meaning is nearly the same. The KJV's "and to his children" supplies the "and" in translation; it is not a witness to the other reading. The Plain English follows Kings.

p: Kings has a place name, Zair. Chronicles has "with his commanders," which in Hebrew looks almost the same.

readings.w: Masoretic Text of Kings (Leningrad Codex); KJV
2 Chronicles 21:9 (Masoretic Text)
readings.plain: Joram went across with his commanders

why: The Hebrew letters of "to Zair" (ts'yrh) and "with his commanders" ('m-sryw) are close, and one probably arose from the other. Chronicles may have smoothed an unknown place name. The Plain English follows Kings, which is the older text, and leaves Zair as a place whose location is not known.

p: Kings makes Ahaziah 22 when he became king; Chronicles says 42, which would make him older than his father.

readings.w: Masoretic Text of 2 Kings 8:26; Septuagint of Kings; most versions
2 Chronicles 22:2 (Masoretic Text; KJV); some Greek manuscripts of Chronicles read twenty, others twenty-two

why: His father Jehoram became king at thirty-two and ruled eight years (8:17), so he died at forty. A son of forty-two is impossible, and nearly everyone agrees that the number in Chronicles is a copyist's error, perhaps from confusing number signs. The Plain English follows Kings. Those who hold that Scripture is without error in its original manuscripts usually explain the Chronicles number this way.
